book.title: The Linux Programming Interface
book.author: Michael Kerrisk
book.baseline: The book discusses Linux through 2.6.35. Source checkpoints are verified separately against Linux 7.2.11.
book.usage: Reading references only. The book PDF and its examples are not distributed. All explanations and experiments here are original companion material; this project is unaffiliated with the author or publisher.

glossary.program: Executable code and data that can be run. A process is an execution of a program.
glossary.process: An executing program together with identity and state such as memory, credentials and open descriptors.
glossary.task: Linux’s schedulable execution context. A multithreaded process has multiple tasks.
glossary.file descriptor: A small integer indexing an entry in a process’s descriptor table.
glossary.open-file description: The underlying open-file state, including the offset and file status flags, referred to by one or more descriptor entries.
glossary.fork: An interface that creates a child process. It returns in both parent and child on success, with different return values.
glossary.exec: The family of interfaces that replace the current process’s program image.
glossary.close-on-exec: A descriptor flag, FD_CLOEXEC, requesting that the descriptor be closed during successful program replacement.
glossary.system call: An interface through which a user program asks the kernel to perform an operation. A library wrapper is a separate layer.
glossary.virtual address space: The address-space view used by a process. Equal virtual addresses across processes need not imply shared ordinary variable state.
glossary.copy-on-write: An implementation technique that can defer copying private memory pages until a write requires a separate copy.
glossary.exit status: Encoded information about how a child terminated; decode it with the appropriate wait-status macros.
glossary.zombie: A terminated task whose remaining exit information has not yet been collected or otherwise disposed of.

lessons.title: A new process, inherited access
lessons.reading: Read a few paragraphs of the Processes section. Stop when the relationship between a parent and child gives you a question.
lessons.summary: Follow one open file through fork and program replacement.
lessons.prompt: A launcher opens a file, forks, and the child executes a helper. What access might the helper still have?
explanation: An open descriptor is an entry in a process’s descriptor table. After an ordinary fork, the child has its own table with inherited entries referring to the same open-file descriptions.

Closing the child’s descriptor removes that entry from the child’s table. The parent’s entry remains open. Replacing the child’s program with exec normally preserves open descriptors; FD_CLOEXEC requests closure on successful exec.

A fresh PID or program image does not by itself remove inherited authority. Descriptor handling is one part of a launcher’s boundary; credentials, namespaces and other inherited state deserve their own investigation later.
lessons.follow_up: If the parent closes its copy after fork, which process still has a reference to the open file?
lessons.boundary: The application calls fork and execl through its C library. The indexed calls below are inside the kernel. The connection across those layers is a curated explanation, not a compiler-resolved edge from the experiment.

experiment.intro: An optional experiment using a temporary, immediately unlinked file containing only “demo only”. No privileges or sensitive files are involved.
experiment.expected:
default: helper inherited descriptor=yes data=demo only
--cloexec: helper inherited descriptor=no
--close-child: helper inherited descriptor=no
all three: parent descriptor still open=yes
experiment.observe: Compare what the helper can read with whether the parent’s descriptor remains open. The closed descriptor is one piece of state, not a general clean slate.

lessons.title: What does a process ID identify?
lessons.reading: Use Chapter 2 for the broad idea. When you reach Chapter 6, compare a program’s identity with the state the kernel tracks for it.
lessons.summary: Connect getpid to the task Linux is currently running.
lessons.prompt: If two executions run the same program, what makes them different processes?
explanation: A program is executable code and data; a process is an execution with identity and state. Two executions can run the same program while having distinct process IDs.

In Linux, a task is a schedulable execution context. Threads add a distinction: getpid returns a thread-group ID, while gettid identifies the calling thread. You can leave thread details until the relevant reading.
A PID is an identifier. Access control depends on additional state; possessing a new number is not an isolation mechanism.
lessons.follow_up: After a successful exec, would you expect the PID to change? Keep that prediction for the program-replacement topic.
lessons.boundary: getpid in the C program is an application-facing interface. The macro-generated kernel handler is a separate layer. This index covers the kernel, not the C library wrapper.

experiment.intro: Print the current process ID and its parent’s ID. Repeat the command if you are curious.
experiment.expected:
pid=<a process ID> parent=<its parent’s ID>
pid=<another process ID> parent=<its parent’s ID>
experiment.observe: Values depend on the running system. Repeated invocations often share a parent. PID reuse is possible over time.

lessons.title: Two processes, two variable values
lessons.reading: When you reach fork, read its return-value behavior and memory semantics. This is a later-reading option, not a prerequisite for continuing Chapter 2.
lessons.summary: Separate inherited contents from continuing to share ordinary variable changes.
lessons.prompt: A child changes an ordinary variable after fork. What value would the parent print after waiting for that child?
explanation: Ordinary fork creates separate virtual address spaces with initially equivalent contents. A later assignment to an ordinary private variable in the child does not change that variable in the parent.
Linux can implement this efficiently using copy-on-write. Separate logical state does not require eagerly copying every physical page. Explicit shared mappings are a different case.
copy_mm distinguishes sharing an address space with CLONE_VM from duplicating memory-management state. The local branch explains a choice; it is not the whole copy-on-write implementation.
lessons.follow_up: Why can the virtual addresses match even though later values differ?
lessons.boundary: The C library’s fork wrapper is outside this index. These checkpoints investigate kernel memory setup; they do not trace an observed run of the experiment.

experiment.intro: The parent waits so the two output lines have a predictable order.
experiment.observe: Compare the assignment in the child branch with the value printed in the parent branch.

lessons.title: Two descriptors, one file position
lessons.reading: Read the file-sharing discussion when it fits your reading. Compare descriptor-table entries with open-file descriptions.
lessons.summary: Explore the shared object beneath an inherited descriptor.
lessons.prompt: The child reads the first two bytes of a file. After waiting, which byte will the parent read through its inherited descriptor?
explanation: After fork, the inherited descriptor entries refer to the same open-file description. That description holds the file offset, so a read by one process can advance the position observed by the other.
The parent waits for the child in this experiment to avoid racing reads. The result is a shared-offset observation, not a scheduling puzzle.
Duplicating the descriptor table preserves references to file objects. That differs from opening the pathname again to obtain a separate open-file description.
lessons.follow_up: What would you predict if the child opened the pathname independently instead?
lessons.boundary: These are compiler-resolved calls inside the kernel. The explanation linking descriptor references to the experiment is a teaching annotation, not a runtime trace.

experiment.intro: Use a temporary, unlinked four-byte file. The child reads two bytes before the parent reads one.
experiment.observe: A parent result of c follows the child’s read of a and b. Both processes close their own descriptors.

checkpoints.title: Follow descriptor-table duplication
checkpoints.notice: The dup_fd call duplicates the table for this path.
checkpoints.ignore: CLONE_FILES is a distinct sharing option; ordinary fork does not request it.
checkpoints.question: Does a new table imply new open-file descriptions?

checkpoints.title: Inspect what duplication retains
checkpoints.notice: Read the get_file call and the neighboring assignment into the new table. The code retains a reference to an existing file object.
checkpoints.ignore: The surrounding allocation and resizing mechanics can wait.
checkpoints.question: Which objects are retained by reference?

lessons.title: An exit status the parent can collect
lessons.reading: Read about termination and waiting when you reach those chapters. Keep termination and collecting a child’s status as two separate events.
lessons.summary: Follow cleanup and the parent’s wait operation.
lessons.prompt: A child exits with status 42. What must the parent do to obtain that result?
explanation: The parent can call waitpid to wait for a child and obtain status information. That status is encoded; WIFEXITED checks for normal termination and WEXITSTATUS extracts the exit code.
Termination releases resources, while some information remains available for a parent to collect. The zombie state concerns that retained information, not a process continuing to execute normally.
The example uses _exit in the child. The C library exit function additionally handles library-level cleanup such as stdio flushing; that distinction matters after fork.
lessons.follow_up: What changes if the child terminates because of a signal instead of calling _exit?
lessons.boundary: waitpid and _exit are application interfaces. The indexed Linux wait and exit implementations are separate layers; architecture and C-library wrappers determine the entry route.

experiment.intro: The child calls _exit(42); the parent handles interrupted waits and decodes a normal exit.
experiment.observe: Notice the normal-exit test before extracting the status.

checkpoints.question: Why is cleanup broader than returning an exit number?

checkpoints.ignore: Compatibility wrappers and tracing helpers can wait.
checkpoints.question: Which side of the parent-child relationship is waiting here?

lessons.title: A different program, the same PID
lessons.reading: Read the execve discussion and its descriptor behavior when you reach Chapter 27. Compare program replacement with process creation.
lessons.summary: Observe what is replaced and what can survive exec.
lessons.prompt: A process successfully executes a new program image. Which would you expect to remain: its PID, an ordinary variable’s changed value, or an unmarked open descriptor?
explanation: A successful exec replaces the program image within the existing process. The PID remains, while the new image starts with its own initialized program state.
Open descriptors normally survive unless marked close-on-exec or otherwise closed. Exec does not by itself remove every kind of inherited access.

The experiment executes itself with a different argument. Its second run of main shows the same PID and the initial variable value. Code following a successful execl call is not resumed in the old image.
lessons.follow_up: How would a launcher arrange for a helper to receive only the descriptors it needs?
lessons.boundary: execl is a C-library convenience interface. The kernel-side exec path handles the requested replacement; the library-to-kernel transition is a curated conceptual bridge.

experiment.intro: Run the program by its local path. It replaces itself once, using a marker argument.
experiment.expected:

after exec pid=<same ID> value=7
experiment.observe: Compare the two PIDs and the initialization of the ordinary variable.
